theme: Hear the voice of my pleas for mercy
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 28. It begins with a desperate cry and ends with a shout of praise. Notice what changes between verse 5 and verse 6.
settingTheScene: Psalm 28 is a psalm of David. He is surrounded by wicked people and fears being swept away with them. He cries to the LORD, his rock, and asks for justice. Halfway through there is a change: he hears the answer, and the psalm ends in praise and a prayer for God’s people.
observation: “To you, O LORD, I call; my rock, be not deaf to me” (v. 1).
“Hear the voice of my pleas for mercy, as I cry to you for help” (v. 2).
“Do not drag me off with the wicked” (v. 3).
“Because they do not regard the works of the LORD, or the work of his hands, he will tear them down and build them up no more” (v. 5).
“Blessed be the LORD! For he has heard the voice of my pleas for mercy” (v. 6).
“The LORD is my strength and my shield; in him my heart trusts, and I am helped” (v. 7).
“The LORD is the strength of his people; he is the saving refuge of his anointed” (v. 8).
“Oh, save your people and bless your heritage! Be their shepherd and carry them forever” (v. 9).
interpretation:
David’s fear is silence. “If you are deaf to me, I become like those who go down to the pit.” He cannot bear the thought that God might not answer. He lifts his hands toward the holy sanctuary, and asks God not to treat him as he treats the wicked, whose speech is smooth but whose hearts are full of evil.

He prays for justice in verse 4, asking that they receive what their deeds deserve. This is not personal revenge. It is the cry for a righteous God to act against evil. The reason is verse 5: they do not regard the works of the LORD. They ignore him and act as though no one will answer.

Then, without a transition, the mood changes. “Blessed be the LORD! For he has heard the voice of my pleas for mercy.” Between verses 5 and 6, something has happened. Perhaps a priest spoke a word of assurance, or perhaps David simply felt the burden lift. Whatever it was, he now says, “The LORD is my strength and my shield; in him my heart trusts, and I am helped; my heart exults, and with my song I give thanks to him.”

The final verses widen the circle. The LORD is not just his strength but “the strength of his people.” He is the saving refuge of his anointed. And David asks for the whole flock: “Save your people and bless your heritage. Be their shepherd and carry them forever.” The same shepherd who walked with David is asked to carry all his people.

Jesus is the final Shepherd and the final Anointed. He cried out to his Father in distress and was heard. And now he carries his flock.
connection: Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34 describe the LORD as shepherd. Psalm 18:2 uses the same strength and shield language. Psalm 22:24 says he has not hidden his face but has heard when he cried to him. John 10:11-16 shows Jesus as the Good Shepherd. Hebrews 5:7 says Jesus offered up prayers with loud cries and tears, and was heard. 1 Peter 5:4 speaks of the Chief Shepherd.
application:
Take a burden to the LORD today, and keep praying until you can, like David, bless him.

Pray verse 9 for your church: save your people, bless them, shepherd them, and carry them.

Thank God for a time he heard you when you felt unheard.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to hear your pleas for mercy.
Thank him that he is your strength and shield.
